_note: What to generate next, in priority order. `npm run pixellab -- --list` prices a run without spending anything; a run generates every subject that has no sheet yet. Descriptions are THE SUBJECT ONLY — the style anchor carries palette, outline weight, shading and colour count, and a long style suffix actively fights it.
_budget: Pro tools cost 20 generations each against 2,000/month. Check the live figure with get_balance before a batch rather than trusting this line. THE CONCURRENCY LIMIT IS 8 JOBS, not a time window: fire eight, they finish in about nine minutes, fire eight more. There is no cooldown to wait out.
_fieldRule: Anything that reaches the game FIELD must end up 32x32; generate larger and use PixelLab's Unzoom, or generate at 32 directly. Card icons are exempt and 64px is better — a card window zooms by integers and wants the detail.
_next: For directional field art the pipeline is: generate one side view here, then 'Generate 8 rotations', then 'Animate with text' for the walk. Those are separate tools and are not automated by this script yet.

_characterNote: The CHARACTER BUILDER is a separate pipeline from this queue and is not run by `npm run pixellab`. Characters are generated once, get a character id, and are then animated as states of that id -- so a walk, an attack and a death are the same figure rather than three drawings that resemble each other. See docs/PIXELLAB.md. It needs a `pixellabRig` block in art/sprites.json before anything it produces can be packed, and that rig must be written against a real generated sheet rather than guessed from the docs.

_characterRecipe._note: Claude Design's settings for the character builder. Not defaults -- set them by hand. Full write-up and the prompt template in docs/PIXELLAB.md.
promptShape: body itemised, and the POSE stated explicitly -- an action pose cannot be animated into a different one
a line of authorial intent (what the player should read this as)
_characterRecipe.differsFromIcons: Icons take the SUBJECT ONLY; a style suffix fights the anchor. Characters DO carry palette and outline direction, because there is far more surface for the model to drift on.

_apiNote: VALIDATED against the live API on 2026-08-15. Two icons generated end to end and wired in (work_boots, feed_sack) at 20 generations each. Two things worth knowing that the handoff could not have: the style anchor can be passed as `style_image_url` pointing at this repo's own raw.githubusercontent URL, which avoids a 25KB base64 argument entirely -- the repo being public makes it its own asset host. And create_image_pro returns each candidate as a SEPARATE file, not the web UI's 4x4 sheet, so pixellab-cut's `icon` command does not apply; `npm run cut -- single <src> <dst>` was added for that path.
_styleAnchorNote: THE ANCHOR IS A SHEET OF FARM PRODUCE, and with the default style_copy (all four of color_palette, outline, detail, shading) the model copies its SUBJECT as well as its rendering. The first oak came back as four pumpkins and an onion. For anything that is not a small hand-held object, pass style_copy WITHOUT "detail" -- palette, outline and shading carry the look, and detail is what drags the anchor content across. Same prompt, same anchor, detail dropped: a correct oak, first try.
_modelNote: create_image_pro is 20 generations and returns a SET -- 64 candidates at <=42px, 16 at <=85px, 4 at <=170px, 1 above. 64x64 is the sweet spot: 16 candidates for one price, and enough resolution for a card. Going to 128px to get a bigger sprite costs you twelve of the sixteen tries, which is exactly when a bad generation has nowhere to hide. Generate small, draw at an integer zoom. The cheaper models (pixen at 1 generation, pixflux for img2img/forced palette) are the right call for simple flat objects; pro earns its cost on anything with form.
_pickNote: npm run fetch -- <job-id> <name> pulls every candidate plus a 4-across contact sheet into assets/pixellab/sheets/<name>/. Look at the contact sheet, then npm run cut -- single <sheet>/<name>_NN.png assets/pixellab/picked/<name>.png. Keep every candidate: they are paid for, and the first cell picked has more than once not been the best one.

_ranchRoster._note: THE OWNER'S OWN ANIMALS. These are real animals on a real ranch and the point is that the game has them in it. Side views are GENERATED AND STAGED in assets/pixellab/picked/ -- fjord_pony, arabian_horse, draft_mule, donkey, rooster_big. rooster_big is wired (the yard scene). The other four are not wired to anything yet, deliberately: a side view is a reference, not an enemy.
_ranchRoster._whatIsMissing: A field animal needs eight facings and a walk, not one profile. The path is: create_8_direction_object (or create_character for anything humanoid) using the staged side view as a reference image, then animate the walk, then npm run cut -- cell / strip onto the game grid. That is a different and more expensive tool than the icon recipe, and it has not been run on an animal yet.
_ranchRoster._sizeRule: Field art ends at 32x32. These were generated at 64 for the candidate count; unzoom or regenerate at 32 before packing, and do NOT scale a 64px sprite down in CSS -- it breaks the pixel grid.

_horrorPlan._note: MAKE THE WHOLE CAST SCARY, the way the farmhand already is. The infected farmhand is the one piece of this that is finished and it is the enemy you see most in a run; everything else infected is still an ordinary animal wearing a CSS filter, and it looks like it.
_horrorPlan._whatWorks: The farmhand was made with Characters -> Create from Text, Humanoid, Pro, character size 40 custom, camera Low Top-Down, with limezu_character_ref.png and limezu_style_char_128.png as references, then the Scary Walk 8-frame preset. Full recipe in docs/PIXELLAB.md. Use the FARMHAND ITSELF as the Style Character for everything infected that follows -- that is what makes a cast rather than a collection.
_horrorPlan._order: Do the animals the player meets most first. The infected side views for hen, rooster, hog and sheep are generated and staged; they are references for the 8-direction pass, not shippable enemies.
_horrorPlan._pairing: Every horror version should be generated FROM its healthy counterpart as a reference image, so the two read as the same animal before and after. That is the whole horror premise of the game and it does not survive generating them independently.

_mapsAndTilesets._note: OWNER WANTS MORE MAPS. Logged to think through before generating, because this is the first thing on the list that changes the GAME rather than the art.
_mapsAndTilesets._whatTheSeedActuallyDoes: Right now the seed drives enemy spawns, elite rolls, drops, offer-pool draws and crop scatter -- everything that goes through the mulberry32 RNG. It does NOT pick a map, because there is one arena: a flat terrain bake with crop nodes scattered on it. Same ground every run. So "maps spawn randomly on the seed" is not true yet; making it true is a real feature, not a content drop.
_whatItWouldTake: A map descriptor in content: tileset, ground bake, node mix, hazard flavour, arena size.
The terrain bake reading that descriptor instead of the one hardcoded set.
The seed choosing a map, which means the map choice must be the FIRST draw off the RNG -- anything else and adding a map silently changes every existing seed replay.
A test that the same seed still replays identically, which is a non-negotiable in this project.
_mapsAndTilesets._generationSide: PixelLab does have the tools for this: create_topdown_tileset for whole ground sets, create_path_tiles for tracks and dirt roads, create_map_object for props, and animate_object for the twinkle. An animated gem seam or a plant that moves is exactly what create_object_state / animate_object are for, and it would make a harvest node read as worth standing on before you commit to standing there -- which is the mining design already in place.
_mapIdeas: the home quarter at dusk (what exists)
the blighted field, dead trees and ash
the creek bottom, water and mud that slows
the night pasture, lit only by burn barrels
_mapsAndTilesets._doFirst: Do NOT generate a tileset until the map descriptor exists. A tileset with nowhere to go is the most expensive kind of art to have made.

_classifierNote: A generation request for the Boot Knife was once refused by the CLAUDE CODE permission classifier -- the agent harness, not PixelLab. The prompt never reached the API. Retrying the identical request went straight through and returned sixteen good knives. If a generation is refused, check WHICH layer refused it before rewriting the prompt: the wording was never the problem.
